utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am. Welcome back to the Tribunal. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Teufika Ibrahimefendic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have testified before this Tribunal on four previous occasions: Namely, in the Krstic case, on 27 July 2000; in the Plavsic case, in December of 2002; in the Tolimir case, in February of 2011; and, most recently, in the Karadzic case, on 22nd March 2012.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you confirm that you've recently had an opportunity to listen to the testimony you gave in the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you recall discussing with me that you wished to make a correction to that testimony; namely, to portion of it found at transcript page 5830, where you are recorded as having stated at lines 7 to 8, and I quote: "But there isn't a single family in Zvornik, for, example, that hasn't 20 male members of its family missing." And you wish to make clear that you were given -- giving an example of one family who had 20 male members missing and not that all families in Zvornik had 20 male members missing. Is that a correction you wish to make to your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the correction. But yesterday, while I was listening to the material, there was another sentence, saying that in one family, 20 persons went missing. The context was the following. A Judge asked me whether there were similar traumas in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to which I replied in the affirmative. That there were people missing in Zvornik, and that, in one family, 20 had gone missing, but not as many as in the families in, say, Srebrenica. That's what I would like to add. Otherwise, I agree with the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And taking into account the -- these corrections that you've just made, and bearing in mind that the evidence that you gave in the Krstic case related to your knowledge of the conditions of women and children and survivors of the Srebrenica events, related to what was known in 2000, can you confirm that the evidence you gave in -- to the Krstic Chamber was true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was information about patients, clients in the year 2000. That's what I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if you were asked today about those same matters, would you provide the -- this Court with the same information, again bearing in mind, that it was related to what was known in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, normally I would tender the -- her prior testimony from the Krstic case, which is 65 ter 29099. However, I am mindful of your decision of 1st July in which there was an instruction to postpone the tendering of her testimony until the completion -- until she completes her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is clear and it's on the record that you have the intention to tender the material. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll proceed with a very brief summary of her prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we proceed, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, are you -- is your chair comfortable or is it moving and not very comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Mr. President, I'll proceed then with a brief summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Teufika Ibrahimefendic is a psychotherapist who has treated women and children traumatised by the war. Since 1994 she has worked for the Vive Zene organisation which is a multi-disciplinary organisation specialising in the treatment of victims of war, including hundreds of women and children traumatised by the July 1995 events of Srebrenica. The witness previously testified about the effects of the trauma on the Srebrenica victims. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any additional questions, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, if we can just begin covering a bit more of your background since 2000. Since you testified in the Krstic case, is it correct that you have continued to practice as a psychotherapist?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And while you were the psycho-social ^ co-ordinator of the Vive Zene, can you tell us what position you currently hold in that same organisation?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Apart from my daily psychotherapeutic work, I'm also training co-ordinator. That is, I'm in charge of the training programmes at Vive Zene. We train both our own staff and professionals from other organisations, such as social workers, psychologists, police officers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now the Vive Zene organisation, does it continue to receive funding from the European Commission and the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We receive funding from the European community but now no longer from the Dutch ministry. Instead, we receive funding from a Swiss organisation, then from Norway, from UNDP, the UN for victims of torture. I'm speaking mostly about donations from these organisations and countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And since the year 2000, has the Vive Zene organisation become more active in dealing with -- in dealing with recovery from trauma at a community level, as it pertains to the Srebrenica victims?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, since 1994, when our organisation was founded, we mostly worked with individual patients. But in the past ten years or so, we have worked intensively in the community. We work with groups or families but also with other groups. We do not only work with women who were victims of violence but also with other victims of torture. Now our multi-disciplinary team has 16 members, of whom six are psychologists, three are pedagogists, then we also have doctors, nurses, social workers, and a social pedagogue. We have widen our activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: We also -- we're also active in the legal field. We're trying to bring about changes of laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, besides your co-ordinating and management responsibilities, have you continued to carry your own case load of -- of treating patients? Have you continued to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question already seems to have been answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't think we got the end of that. Could you just repeat what you were going to say. All we got was: "Yes, that's my ..." Did you intend to continue your answer?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: That's my basic task - treating patients. That's what I do at Vive Zene.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And are you still a member of the European Association for Psychotherapists?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you also continue to -- have you also continued to be a member of the European Association of Gestalt Psychotherapy?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that you -- sorry. I'll -- I'll rephrase that. Have you worked with -- do you continue to work with both Serb and Bosnian victims of the war?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And since your -- and since -- well, in the last 13 years, can you tell us whether you've treated women who suffer from the Srebrenica Syndrome?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And those women that you've treated that suffer from the Srebrenica Syndrome, do they still live in the state of uncertainty, as you've described it in your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Many things have changed since I gave testimony in 2013 [as interpreted]. There have been changed in the field of individual trauma and also collective trauma. Since 1995, when I began to work with women who were put up in Tuzla after being expelled from Srebrenica, there have been both similarities and differences between individuals. But one can say that from the initial traumatisation characterised by panic, fear and uncertainty, gave way to the confusion and lack of understanding, due to the fast changes. Then there was grief due to loss. The traumatic event that happened in 1995 in Srebrenica is an original, a basic event, but everything that happened later made the victims go through their own individual process which was also a group process and one characteristic of the whole community. At first, I focussed on individual symptoms, because, at that time, the victims mostly complained of their problems and the symptoms they could not understand and had a very hard time coping.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, if I could stop you right there. Can you tell us more precisely, the women who suffer from the Srebrenica Syndrome who still not found -- have not had their loved one's remains identified, can you describe their condition to us? Those women who today still don't have those identifications.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I was going to say that. Now, the main feature of that trauma is grief and sorrow and deep suffering because their loved ones still have not been identified. The search for the mortal remains is still ongoing. Nearly 8.000 people in Bosnia-Herzegovina still haven't found their nearest and dearest. The traumatic reactions have to do with grief and sorrow and the problem of stopping these. Because the bodies still haven't been found and then the real mourning cannot begin. And when I say "mourning," I mean the beginning of a recovery. Although many women have learned to live with these symptoms and accepted their life as it is in their own way, but that doesn't mean that they aren't still suffering.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Based on your observations in treating these women, can you just briefly describe for us how they envision their future.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: In the context of their overall physical and mental health, it is very difficult to hear from them how they see their future. They still don't have a vision because everything is connected with the dead, with mourning, with current illnesses in the family, with loss, and it's very difficult for them to imagine their future and distance themselves from the dramatic event. As much as the therapist or anyone else may wish to help them to establish distance from the past, they always go back to it. So it's a very difficult task to build that distance and have them focus on the future. They feel that they need more information, that they need to learn the truth, and they need support from others, from the community, and that others must understand and acknowledge their suffering. That is necessary for relations with others to develop in the direction of trust. Because that's a very -- that's a significant difficulty. They don't trust anybody. And they have difficulties in contacts with others. And some women still have problems with themselves. So that it's hard on them. The traumatic process still has not finished, and it's difficult for them to build a vision of the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, when you testified in Krstic, you explained that when these women receive certificates confirming the death of their relative, they get re-traumatised at that point. There's a bit of a regression and then they can begin a -- the process of, as you just said, mourning. Can you explain whether once these women receive the confirmation of the death of their relatives, whether they're grieving process after that point is the same or different to the normal grieving process, for example, if I were to lose a parent in -- in normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The phenomenon of missing persons is a separate issue not only in Bosnia-Herzegovina but worldwide. When one says a person had gone missing and there's no information of their whereabouts, the people are, of course, under the pressure of finding that person. But once the mortal remains are found and once they are faced with the results of DNA analysis, still a good portion of them cannot believe that it is the person. That is why it is very difficult to speak of it in terms of regular grieving or mourning. It is a fact that many women who even managed to locate their nearest and dearest, especially in terms of mothers who found their children, they exhibit signs of relief. They are relieved because the mortal remains of their near and dear have finally been found. Although there is this amount of relief, on the other hand they also feel exceptionally sad. They are in disbelief. They still do not want to believe that these are the bones of their child. The loss of a child is one of the most difficult losses. So to speak of it in terms of regular grieving, like when one has lost a parent who was 85 years old, the death of that person is accepted as part of loss, normal loss in life. But in the case of the missing, one cannot speak of it that way, because there's always this doubt. There's always a degree of unclarity. A number of issues, questions, that cannot be answered by those left behind, in terms of how that person died, whether they were tortured, whether they were alone, scared, hungry, thirsty, et cetera. There's a number of different circumstances surrounding such deaths which burden those who had lost their family members. On the other hand, though, there is this degree of relief once the mortal remains are found because there is a place they can go to. They can go to the grave. And they have a feeling of some kind of contact with someone who was very close to them, something that belongs to them. It's a place of mourning, a place of relieving one's sadness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you've mentioned the children, and you mentioned those children that were lost. But as pertains to the children who are survivors of the Srebrenica events, you've previously testified about the symptoms they exhibited in the Krstic case. Now, can you tell us today in the last 13 years, how -- how are those -- how are the children doing? Do they still suffer from difficulties?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Children develop, and in the course of that development, they have an opportunity to receive support and to learn many new things in life, to shape their personality so that one part of their identity can remain normal, so to speak. However, there's always a missing part in that identity. There's a void which is never to be filled. Not because some children did not receive a chance to develop or that some of them did not have these, quote/unquote, normal conditions of development. It is because their parents had been traumatised and because in the family circle there was always talk of things past. That is why such children often live in the past, together with their parents. If the children listen to the stories of their parents who talk about their helplessness, about their feeling of not being able to do anything, then the children, in the present, look for some kind of strength to try and pull out their parent from this helplessness. In that part of their identity, there's confusion, which makes their growth and development difficult. It is additionally made difficult because there wasn't sufficient discussion of what happened. The children cannot reconstruct the events themselves because they don't know what happened in July 1995. But at least feelings should have been discussed. They should have been able to talk about what they went through, how they felt, how they were being taken care of, fed, and clothed. But all such basic information was withheld, and the children remained living in this empty space without a sufficient degree of understanding. What is particularly pronounced is that the children were overprotected by their parents on the one hand, whilst, on the other hand, the children had a lot of fear for their mothers. That is why they took care of their mothers. They exhibited adult properties in terms of taking care of their mother, and the mother assumed the role of the child. It is particularly important to stress that if there's a son missing in the family and the other one is still alive, then the children, if they were small, and the mother kept crying and talking about the missing son, the remaining son felt unimportant or less important, and such children often avoided their mothers because they were depressed and sad and kept repeating sad stories and yet the children needed support. They needed something else that they would have received in normal families.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, if I can ask you more specifically, you've had the chance now for some -- sometime since your Krstic testimony to observe some of the children, their development and growth. Can you tell us what, if any, impact the absence of the male population, the fathers, the uncles, you've mentioned the brothers already, has on their development?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I had occasion to follow - and I can say now that I believe the basic traumatic situation is the same - but they developed in different directions. I'd say that the development, in lay terms, may have appeared normal. However, such children have a completely different self-image and a different view of the world, as well as of the others. Privately they say that they are not as worthy, that their self-esteem is low. There are differences, though. Some of them are introvert and very much attached to the family; whereas others are often outside the home, away from the family, seeking support with others. There's a number of delinquent children in such families who had their family members missing. Recently we conducted research and out of 33 delinquent children, nine of them had previously exhibited such behaviour. But when I worked with them they said, "My father had gone missing, my father had been killed." It was the first problem they mentioned even without me asking. The consequence of it is that it is difficult to foresee. There is a number of researchers working on it, some associates of mine as well. But in order to provide a broad estimate that is well nigh impossible at this point in time. I can cite an example. I worked with a student of electrical engineering who was very young when he arrived from Srebrenica with his mother and three sisters. He asked for help. He has a healthy degree of humour and even very serious situations become translated into something humourous by him, but he sought assistance because he had problems with exams. Occasionally he had problems when having to take an oral exam and he wondered why. Sometimes he problems with written tests, but he believed that most of his peers do not have such greet fear when written tests are on hand. Yet he has sweaty palms, palpitations and all that when he needs to take a written test, and he failed such tests several times. We had a number of sessions and at the last session he said, "I am in a state of chaos and I'm well familiar with the theory of chaos." I was quite puzzled and he explained to me, saying, "It is when I was there, it is when I was pushed into the bus and when my mother screamed from the far end of the bus, looking for me." This means that in the course of my work I am still only investigating. It is part of psychotherapeutic work that each patient should arrive at an idea of why things are happening to him. When he managed to establish this link with his past, this image that he painted for me which was so convincing, the picture of this bus, the people, him being in panic, he called it chaos. And I often hear it from my women patients who say, "There was chaos, there was chaos." So based on that example I can say so. I have a number of other examples but this is the one that came to mind first.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, what can you tell us about the -- the desire of the children or young adults, the women, to re-establish life in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Their psychological problems, from their point of view, well, they want to go back. They want to resume their lives there on the one hand. On the other, they refuse to go back. In traumatic states, often things are contradictory and people are always in extremes. On the one hand, there's this exceptionally strong wish, whereas on the other, there is much fear and resistance to going back, as if there were two people. One who -- well, psychologically, one could even say there are two people. One who has this enormous wish to go back to the previous life, including all the people they had shared their beautiful moments with. And, on the other hand, they are well aware of the situation, and the other part is suffering greatly. So there's always this dis-balance or imbalance, the interruption of this continuum of life in Srebrenica. It was traumatic event because a trauma means discontinuation of one's life. It is difficult to pick it up from where you left it. It is even impossible. They need to continue leaving in the future and yet their perception of time is constant. It's as if things froze back then. They are alive but not with deep awareness or enjoying their lives. They are living here but instead of being here, they are back there. And they keep going back. And yet it's 2013. How is one to view that situation from this perspective? When one thinks of 1995 or 1992, how are such experiences to be integrated so as to make them a part of your life, of your life experience, so that you can start anew but at the place where you were born. It's very difficult. And many people from Srebrenica are dispersed. They only come back in summertime for vacation, and often are -- we are visited by our former clients. They talk about their lives in the US, in New Zealand. They do talk, but I think, except for those who had truly undergone this psychotherapeutic treatment, as a person cannot deal with a trauma of that kind alone, it can only be dealt with in contact with others, through communication. So those difficult emotions, those terrifying sentiments need to take shape in -- in the shape of words, in hearing another person accept it. Only in such cases one can expect that they would go back to the place from which they had been driven away. Let me add this. It is not only the case of Srebrenica. It is the case with all other people who survived and left their hearths during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, I just have a couple of final questions, one of which is very short. If I could ask you to briefly answer it. You said -- you just testified that the women who received treatment -- but there are some women who receive treatment. Can you confirm whether or not there are a number of women who have not -- or whether your organisation is capable of handling all of the women that require treatment as a result of the Srebrenica events.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Of course not. But more and more people are being trained in the community to recognise the symptoms of Srebrenica so that such trauma is not denied. People now know where to send them to, where to get help. Because everyone thinks trauma should be dealt with by doctors. That it's a medical condition, that the post-traumatic stress disorder is a psychiatric diagnosis. It's not. They're not sick. They are not psychiatric patients. They have issues that can be dealt with. So the organisation alone cannot cover everyone. We are increasing our capacity, the volume of our work, we also train and supervise others, and we instruct people to go to appropriate institutions. Of course, many of those people do not wish to be helped, in the sense that they think no one can help them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Finally, if I can ask you just how these women and children and survivors of the Srebrenica events, how -- how have they done in the last 13 years based on your observations, in terms of re-establishing community relationships?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: In my experience, and from my point of view based on my practice thus far, I could put it this way: As of 2003, when the burial of mortal remains started takes place in Srebrenica, through the years, their psychological situation has peaks and troughs, both psychologically and physically, actually. For example, there's a period where they receive notification of identification, when they go to such centres where they have to identify the mortal remains or accept them as the missing person. Next follows the stage of preparing for burial and then the period of calming down and performing rituals. When such women come, their main topic that they begin their story with is what happened in their immediate family and their extended family, and they always, or for the most part, talk about death. Of course, there is the other part which they do not easily lend to inspection that they do live, that occasionally they smile, laugh, or experience joy, but everything is intermixed with death. Say, a grandchild is born. They mourn because of those who are no longer present, saying they could have seen this, they could have been witness to it. There's always something that they miss. I keep offering life, and they keep coming back with death, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. I think the best to do would to take the break now and not start cross-examination yet. Ms. Ibrahimefendic, we take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after that, when the Defence will cross-examine you. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You'll find him to your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Ibrahimefendic.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, I'd like to ask you the following: Did the Prosecution of this Tribunal ask that you draft a written expert report for the needs of this case, about the matters you are to testify to today?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nor were you asked to produce a report for the Tolimir case and your testimony there.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you be prepared to draft a written report?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't see what the purpose of it would be. I think I've provided sufficient information through my testimony. It would need a thorough explanation, in terms of why it is needed, to what end, for whom, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If it were explained to you, you would be prepared to draft such a report; correct?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I would gladly accept to draft a report together with my colleagues so that it would be a report produced by the Vive Zene Therapeutic Centre. I would rather accept that than working on my own. I'm a member of a multi-disciplinary team. Each team member, including the physician, the psychologist, the pedagogue, they all have a role to play, and that is why I would be more inclined to accept an assignment of that nature, in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The way I understand your words is that you think you alone would not be able to explain the situation in totality.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: It's not that. I could explain the total situation, and I would provide my opinion based on my experience and work. But, in order for it to be a report covering several dimensions, it would take team approach. My role would be the greatest, I believe, but I would still prefer it to be a multi-disciplinary approach. Trauma which follows disasters caused by people is a complicated process which requires including as many professionals as possible to have a total picture of all events and processes taking place at an individual, group, ethnic, and community level. I believe it would be of great assistance to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Your testimony in the Krstic case was applicable in the circumstances 13 years ago, but one cannot say today that the situation is the same as back then. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I would agree with you, in the sense of individual suffering, but not in any other sense because the time that has elapsed created different problems. We are talking about traumatised people here, and we can't view it all as a single event which took place. What follows is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's precisely the thrust of my question.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: So what follows, all the consequences that are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second. Mr. Lukic, I would say 80 per cent of the examination-in-chief was about what has changed since 2000. Now, what's the use of asking whether anything has been changed? If you have any focussed question, fine. But it's just more or less ignoring what the witness testified about, that a lot of things have changed, and how they changed, and that apparently was part of the focus of the additional questions. So if you have any focussed question on the changes, fine. But to ask whether something changed, that is, I would say, obvious from the examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, just to explain why I asked this question is that because this testimony from Krstic case should be expert analysis in this case if it -- and you are going to decide about the -- that expertise at the end of this testimony. So that's why I'm asking, is that testimony from Krstic case still valid today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you asked whether anything had changed, and things have changed. If you have any specific questions, no problems, Mr. Lukic, but don't ask a question for which we have heard the answer in approximately 35 to 40 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Krstic case, madam, you testified that at Srebrenica, Potocari, boys were separated from women. The age of the boys was, for example, 10 years. How many boys from 10 to 16 years were separated from their mothers?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I have no relevant information. I only worked with some who said that they had been separated but, otherwise, I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have information about boys of that age who moved with the armed column?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the Krstic trial, you mentioned the impossibility to return to Srebrenica, and you mentioned that today as well. Is the situation different nowadays?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Speaking about return, I used that term in the psychological sense. All those who want to return are in a dilemma. They are at a cross-roads. They both want to return and don't want to return. To me, that psychological thing is more of a problem than reconstructing houses and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, return is a very exact notion; right? If a person has returned and lives there, psychology doesn't have much to do with that. Let me ask you: Who is in power at Srebrenica today?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: To the extent I follow the media, the deputy head of municipality is a Bosniak. But he doesn't provide psychological certainty or that they can return. Maybe in reality things are safe, but inside these people are -- are uncertain. They feel unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the majority population at Srebrenica nowadays is Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I really don't know the population structure at Srebrenica. I don't even know how many people there are. I -- in my work, and in our work, such information is not required. We don't need to know how many people live in a municipality. We don't rely on statistical data.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it normal and acceptable that life in Tuzla provides better opportunities for work and education and could that be a reason why many people aren't returning?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: If I look at that from a different angle, I cannot agree with you that opportunities are the reason, because there are schools and university and roads. Because you must bear in mind that nobody will gladly return to a place where they experienced fear. Normal people who had an accident do not like to go near that place where we were helpless and weak. I think that people have permanent traumatic memories. I know a number of people who returned, including Serbs, who used not to live at Srebrenica but now do. I know what they went through to be able to accept the fact that they now live at Srebrenica, and they are going through all the phases of adapting and so on. And it's a big difference -- there's a big difference between living in Sarajevo and living in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the fact that they started a life elsewhere, found a place to live and a job, that their children are going to school, a reason for not returning to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: That is a reason why some people don't return from exile or from other countries. But working with these people - and I had the opportunity to speak to some people who live in Sweden and have everything there that's required for a normal life - but one part of their identity constantly suffers. They cannot forget their previous identity, and it's difficult for them to integrate in the new surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about this, isn't that characteristic of anybody who goes to another country to live there, nostalgia?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is nostalgia but nobody is a refugee of their own free will. Becoming a refugee is preceded by trauma. Somebody who decides to go to another country has the feeling that they have control over their own life, that it was their choice, and anybody else then has the full right to tell such a person, "Yeah, you've got to cope with that. It was your decision." But you cannot compare that with trauma because there was no free choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you conduct research into the differences between persons who are refugees from Sarajevo and others who are refugees from Srebrenica but live in the same country, such as Sweden?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. No, but I'm sure that both suffer, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also true that there are differences within families as to the decision whether they should return or not? Somebody is for and somebody is against.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are discussions in many families, the older family members and the younger family members. Mostly it's the older ones that want to return, but sometimes the younger ones as well. And that can be a source of conflict within the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that sociological problems affect the issue of return greatly, such as no job opportunities, the impossibility to make a living?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. But let me add that if we look at trauma as a process, this sequence, which is a transitional sequence, to call it that, is also characterised by unemployment and shortage of the things you need for life. That is also part of the definition of trauma. In a BH context, apart from expulsion camps, there are also such things as unemployment and uncertainty that are part of trauma, that make up trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe you understand that I'm pausing to let the interpreters do their job.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: War as a sociological and psychological concept has many negative aspects; right?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I would like to add that war causes extreme traumatic experiences, extreme fear. It is something out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree that nobody, even if they don't take part in combat directly, are -- is -- is spared from trauma?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Observers, lookers-on also have traumatic symptoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Prolonged psychological trauma is a condition in which the entire population of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in the first half of the 1990s. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody more, somebody less. But if we speak about Srebrenica, we can speak about cumulative traumatisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, while it was ongoing, gave rise to a lot of hatred among all three peoples?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Speaking to your patients, did you find out that hatred was fertile soil for thoughts of vengeance in the BH population?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I initially didn't call that hatred because that's an emotion which involves a particular type of expression. I saw it more as passion. People feeling passion for their own ethnicity. It was all along the lines: We are one thing, and they are another. There's a clear-cut line of division. Prejudice had existed from before, and that's how huge fear was created. And when people are in fear, they are bound to do things they would never do in a normal, relaxed condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking to your patients, did you hear them speaking about vindictive behaviour on the part of the Serbs against the Muslim population of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. It's very interesting that this concept of vengeance or retaliation was mentioned very rarely. Perhaps because people really don't felt [as interpreted] that way, or because they felt that it was part of their silence and an individual thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Speaking to people - probably mostly to women and children - did you learn why the men decided to break through from Srebrenica instead of surrendering, to try to break through a rather large territory controlled by the VRS? Were they -- did they take that decision out of fear?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I believe that's a question burdening the women too, and -- all those who survived. They described the situation as extremely chaotic, that there was disarray and confusion. People were fleeing toward the UNPROFOR base, expecting protection and help, but no help ever arrived. And these are questions still burdening them. I personally have been unable to get a clear picture of the events. One woman said to me, "This one said this, and then we went there, and then we went to another place," and so on. People were out of their minds. They were beside themselves for fear, and then they make choices that may or may not be right. But, at that given moment, they were the most acceptable to their minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for a clarification. The question was about whether, in your conversations with the women and children, you learned why the men, as Mr. Lukic put it, decided to break through rather than to surrender. In your answer, it's not quite clear to me whether you're describing decisions taken by the women and the children or whether your answer is specifically focussing on the decision taken by the men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It happened in conversation with them, and I can't say the decision was taken this or that way, but most of the women were told, "You go towards Potocari, and we will take to the forest. We'll meet up in Tuzla." I don't know how this all sounds to others now; but, for me, it sounded like it was - how should I put it? - it wasn't a decision-making process. It was made amidst the chaos. They just said, "You go to Potocari, we take to the forest, and we'll meet up in Tuzla." That sentence was frequently used, and it remains etched in my memory. Tuzla was supposed to the place where they would reunite, when they were bidding farewell, where they separated, it was said so. Some people -- some men decided to accompany their women to Potocari because they so decided. And yet some women wanted to go to the forest and were told, "You're a woman. Why would you want to come with us?" That's all I want -- I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't have an answer to the why of that decision. You even doubt whether these were real decisions. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I may add this. They said that their husbands were very frightened and that they did not wish to remain in Srebrenica. They only wanted to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With this addition, when you say that the men were frightened, let me go back to my question. Did they tell you that their husbands were fearful of acts of revenge? Why were they fearful?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, that can come into play. They may have been afraid of that. And there was another sentence that was used: They did not want to fall to Serb hands. That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In such conversations with them, trying to understand this fear by men of being in the Serb hands, did you touch upon the topic of the 28th Division and the massacres of Serb civilians which took place outside Srebrenica? Did you come across that in your trying to understand the process?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not touch upon that topic. The only thing that I personally touched upon was when I worked with a group of women whose husbands were in Srebrenica and they were in Tuzla. As early as 1993, it was UNPROFOR or someone else who transported them to Tuzla, so they were in Tuzla and the men were in Srebrenica. During that period, I had group discussions with the women twice a week. I had never gone to Srebrenica before. They told me of the news they received via ham radio operators that some points that were Dutch-held fell into Serb hands, they mentioned Zeleni Jadar, and then they said that DutchBat withdrew from Jadar. They also said that there were only 5 kilometres left between Jadar and Srebrenica. And then they were informed that another Dutch point fell. And then they said Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second. The question was whether, in your conversations, whether the topic of the 28th Division and massacres of Serb civilians was touched upon. Now you said: "No, I did not touch upon that topic." First of all, are you aware of what the 28th Division is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't. I -- no. The 28th Division? I only learned of that name rather recently, although I can't recall when exactly. I was unaware of the existence of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. And let's try to -- we'd like to receive focussed answers on the questions that were put to you. The question was not about what was Dutch-held or how the fall of Srebrenica developed but it was about your knowledge on the basis of your conversations about the 28th Division and massacres against Serbs. Now, you have answered the question, in terms of the 28th Division, not being aware of that. Do you know anything about massacres against Serbs which had taken place? Mr. Lukic, I take it, close to Srebrenica. That's what you were focussing on. Were you aware of massacres of Serbs or Serbian population of villages close to Srebrenica before Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I learned of it later. I was unaware of it before Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did it play any role in your conversations with the women and the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a bit. Because I put questions concerning the massacres that took place so that I would gain a better picture of everything that went on there and so that I could intervene in trying to put a realistic picture before them so that they could accept it too. But I only learned of this after Srebrenica had fallen, after such discussions with the women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did they tell you about those massacres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, as far as I remember, they -- when they mentioned the massacres, they said they had gone there for food and that it was the main reason why they went to the neighbouring places, especially Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that they denied that massacres had taken place? Or -- I mean, going somewhere for food, in the context of massacres, needs further explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The women did not deny that in conversations. They did say it happened but that they were unaware of particular numbers or of how many. I asked whether there were murders. They said there were but they didn't know how many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will leave this topic, madam. I want to ask you something about your therapy. First of all, I'd like to ask you this: Would you agree with me that your therapeutic sessions helped those who turned to you for help a lot?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The therapy helped so that the people could become more stable so that they could get in touch with themselves, to accept the situation, adapt to the new conditions, and become more resilient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you had much success in treating children too?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We also have a colleague, a lady colleague, who worked a lot with the children, as well as pedagogues, who worked with groups of children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that those who turned for assistance to you are in a much better situation today than they had been in ten or 13 years ago?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I agree. Many women developed a range of abilities to be able to cope with the problems that life put before them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm -- your question was about comparing them immediately after the events, compared to now; or was it about before the events comparing with now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was trying to compare with the time when this lady testified in Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, then it's clear. And I think I understand the answer in that context. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Ibrahimefendic, you mentioned a moment ago some problems. Would you agree that the community needs to provide work, that the political situation needs to become stable? In other words, do social issues deepen the basic problem with the Srebrenica population? A moment ago, you touched upon that topic, but I don't think you have concluded.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I agree, because treating traumatised persons does not begin with or end in the room with the therapist. If an individual is made more resilient, and if they go through their community where they lack the basic means for life, then the psychological help is not as important because other needs need to be met: Social, material, financial, and other needs of the victims. Treating trauma, unfortunately, is still not seen in our parts as a health problem only. It's also a social, legal, economical problem, and all that is required in order to achieve recovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the suffering of these women is made greater by the patriarchal environment they hailed from and that they would have fared much better in coping with it had they come from urban environments where women live under different circumstances and have their professions, occupations?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Trauma affects everyone equally. It's a psychological breakdown, and recovery is individual. It depends on the resources owned by every individual separately. It depends on their life before the war, depends on their capacity or ability acquired prior to the trauma. Recovery, even of educated people, can be very difficult at times if their personal capacity was insufficient to adapt or to cope with such difficult traumatic experiences. Of course, it's easier if one has a profession and if the working part of their personality is re-established and social links with others are established. Then recovery is quicker. But there are educated people who still have problems establishing social ties with others because they had been disrupted. They are full of suspicion, constantly on standby as if standing guard. Irrespective of their level of education, they still share some symptoms which prevent them from being relaxed and feeling free.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you also discussed the inability of these women to remarry. Is it correct that the patriarchal environment that they live in has a bearing on that? And is it also true that, in Bosnia, after the war, there's a chronic lack of males who had either died in the war or left Bosnia after the war?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I said so in 2000. The issue of remarriage is something that can exist even without the war. The war only further complicates the situation, the situation of the shortage of men. With women who have missing family members, they had the problem of finding husbands because they ask, "What am I? I'm not -- I am a widow but I had not been divorced. What am I?" So until their missing are found and identified, the patriarchal surroundings disapproved of such women entering another marriage or establishing similar ties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I actually put two questions in one and the latter part remains unanswered. I was supposed to separate the two. Is it correct that in Bosnia there's a chronic shortage of males, be it because they died in the war or moved out of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Statistics show that there are far more women than men, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that grief because of a lost family member is universal and applies to all of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke to us about traumatic loss, about it being different from a loss that is expected or normal, such as the natural death of a parent. Would you agree with me that the loss of a child in peacetime is also traumatic loss?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. The loss of a child in peacetime is also a traumatic loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that even such traumatic losses produce post-traumatic effects and can continue throughout a person's life?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly the consequences of the loss of a child, both at war and in peace, can cause great differences, can bring about significant differences in the life of a parent or both parents because men and women cope with loss differently. This could be observed during the war too. They both mourn but they display their mourning and their grief differently. So that the loss of a child, both in war and in peace, can cause problems in the relationship between spouses. This, of course, applies to all children who were born and who live in that family, and that can affect the rest of one's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The cases of a breakup of a family after such loss are not rare, are they?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me now go into the results of your research. Is it true that the results of your research are mostly qualitative rather than quantitative in nature?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we also rely on the research made by our colleagues because research is also very expensive and time-consuming, so we rely on quantitative research of our psychiatrist colleagues, both from Bosnia-Herzegovina and from other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your research that is quantified is -- is mostly linked to juvenile delinquency; right?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, that is only one part of it. That research is drawing to an end already. We are co-operating with three faculties from Tuzla and the Basel university. It is research into the occurrence of juvenile delinquency in connection with war-time events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the Keilson model of sequential trauma as developed by Dr. Baker?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, it is sequential trauma.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. He developed a model for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he's our tutor, supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first sequence is the pre-traumatic situation, that is, the pre-refugee status at pre-war times while the person lives a normal life; right?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is necessary for us to understand the differences as compared to the following period.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because if people had -- were exposed to traumatic events before the war, we can assume that they will behave differently in war than if -- than if they hadn't had these traumas, which either make them stronger or weaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have professional contacts with the population of Srebrenica before July 1995?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. It is, however, important to know all stages of a patient's life, from childhood until the traumatic event, or events, that left their imprint or broke -- broke the patient. So that you get a complete image of that person's life ... and for that person to be able to view him or herself in continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you didn't have any control groups to establish the emotional, cognitive, mental, and interpersonal disturbances traumatised people have when compared to those that were not traumatised?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, our team didn't do that, but we relied on the research done by other colleagues who compared persons who have a family member missing and those that don't. There were also persons who found a dead family member and were able to bury him and those that weren't able to. The latter were much more anxious. They were susceptible to panic. They had obsessive syndromes and so on. This research was done last year by a psychiatrist colleague of ours, and we were involved in a way. We processed her information, her input, but she conducted the research basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we've dug too deeply into your area of expertise. I will try to get out because I'm not comfortable there. But it's time for a pause anyway, so we will continue after it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, Mr. Lukic, your previous question referred to persons, people traumatised compared to those who were not traumatised. Now we have been talking about trauma prior to the events in July 1995, and we have spoken about the traumas which were inflicted or occurred as a result of that. I understand the answer to the question such that the question was understood as more or less trauma as a result of the events; that is, with or without missing family members. Did you intend to compare the various levels of traumatisation as a result of the events in 1995; or were you asking about possible existing trauma already at that moment due to prior events?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We established already that there was nobody in Bosnia at that time who was not traumatised, whether directly involved in the conflict or not. I think that Mrs. Ibrahimefendic understood me correctly. And I was trying to compare, to ask about two groups, a group from Srebrenica that was traumatised, and whether she compared those traumas with the population that was general population in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just re-read. At the same time, you say that everyone in Bosnia suffered trauma. So then to ask about comparison between those traumatised and those not traumatised, apparently you wanted to ask and that perhaps is the way in which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Less traumatised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- less -- more or less traumatised by the -- well, let's say by the war events. That is how you understood the question, Ms. Ibrahimefendic? Yes. Then it's clear to me, both now the question and the answer as well. We take a break. Ms. Ibrahimefendic, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can I ask you whether you are on track as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm moving faster. I need just ten more minutes probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten more minutes. Then we take a break, and we will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber understands you would like to raise a preliminary matter. Is that best done now or after we've finished the testimony of Ms. Ibrahimefendic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is very brief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We had spoken with the Defence at the break and it looks like we may be ending earlier than we thought on -- tomorrow and our plan was perhaps we would -- we've agreed that it would be good for us to get together to go over the MFI list and try to narrow that down for our future MFI work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when do you suggest to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if we end early, they're thinking they're going to end before 2.15 so we would get together then. As we don't have any other witnesses -- unless the Court had something else in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Are we talking about today or about tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow. Yes. If you go together over the MFI list that's always highly appreciated and then we will have our list ready as well and see what can be stricken as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one last thing. We had spoken -- I've just spoken to Max Marcus and she would like to come in at the end of the session to help resolve the issue of the witness that you and Mr. Groome spoke of the other day where Victim Witness wanted to put a stop -- we've talked with them. There's an -- I think an agreement with Victim Witness. If she could just get three to four minutes at the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the end of today. Would it then not be best to do that immediately after Ms. Ibrahimefendic has finished her testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine with all of us, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then she's invited to come in ten minutes from now. And then, Ms. Hasan, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: At this stage, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then if Ms. Marcus would be ready to appear in approximately ten minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think she's listening and I will let her know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I would like to inquire whether the Defence whether they have made up their mind already in relation to possible objections to P1790 up to P1799. You have not made up your mind yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could we hear from you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll hear from you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we last spoke about the control group, it was not very clear. I'll read out what -- the transcript to you. On page 39, lines 18 through 21, you say -- I'll read it out in English: "[In English] This research was done last year by a psychiatrist colleague of ours, and we were involved in a way. We processed her information, her input, but she conducted the research basically." [Interpretation] Before last year, you had no control group.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I and my organisation did not but other psychiatrists did, such as children from Tuzla and outside of Tuzla, or children who lost someone and others who don't, and so on. I'm informed of these differences between the control groups and the groups of traumatised persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you one question. A control group, it depends on what exactly you are researching. Is it the effect of the treatment, where you need a control group of persons in a similar situation before the treatment and then not being treated; or treated in another way? I mean, what exactly, Mr. Lukic, did you have in mind when you are asking with control groups?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably I -- I was too broad and maybe I should narrow it down and ask about different groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say a comparative study of some kind. Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For women, for children, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Because a control group, of course, is a very specific scientific concept. But apparently you didn't have that on your mind but whether a comparison was made with people either in different situations or with -- of different age or -- well, whatever. But it was unclear to me what you exactly had on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will -- I will try to clarify it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell us about these control groups. For which area of work did you have them and for which population did your colleague have a control group a year ago?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: She conducted research, the purpose of which to establish the level or the intensity of symptoms in a group who lost or -- a family member. That is, where a family member is missing. She compared the results to the members of a group who were -- there were no family members missing. The result was that the former group -- in the former group, there was much more depression, anxiety, and so on. In other words, the group with missing family members is sicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me if I said that you sympathised with your patients in your work?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Any therapist must have empathy and show understanding for the problems of the patient. Not become a patient himself but at a rational and emotion level understand the feelings of the patient. Without that, you cannot work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me next ask -- ask you if it is true that you based your findings and results exclusively on what you heard from your patients and did not check material matters. You said already that you didn't know how many boys aged 10 to 16 were singled out but you never checked whether that really happened.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I'm a therapist first and foremost and one of the basic ethical principles is that we must trust our patients. We do not establish facts. That is not my job. I deal with the mental and emotional state, how they feel, what they think about, what they notice, what their beliefs are, what went wrong with them, as they say, and that is the purpose of my work, not establishing facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Among the women or children you worked with, were there any women from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: There were several Zepa women. They were taken towards Zenica, for the most part, rather than Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam, thank you for answering our questions. This all we had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I ask again whether Ms. Hasan has any questions, I have one follow-up question related to a -- the question about establishing facts or, rather, whether the results of your findings were exclusively on the basis of what you heard from patients. Now, I'm asking the question in general terms. As a therapist, can it happen that what a patient tells you raises doubts as to the veracity of the story he tells you?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Therapy is a process of long duration. It is a fact that a patient can manipulate in the sense that they say what they believe to be the truth. However, it needn't necessarily be realistic. It is their subjective truth. In order for us to arrive at a point where they can realistically view what had happened, we require a lot of time. They need to accept responsibility for their behaviour and for everything they did as individuals during the period discussed and concerning the problems they have. That means that they need to become aware to gain insight into their behaviour so that their subjective truth could be become objective. Only in that way can a person get in touch with one's own feelings, beliefs, perception, and only then they can establish ties with others. They can connect with others. For as long as they live in a traumatic world of their own, fraught with fear and lack of certitude, they cannot face those events. Some things may remain with the patient, and they can go on living in that kind of reality, but it is important to get that person back into objective reality so that they can ponder their life in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask you the following: In the experience with the Srebrenica -- the persons who you said were traumatised by the Srebrenica events, what -- was it a rare occasion or was it common that your patients had, in the course of the treatment, had to admit that basic facts were perceived wrongly, such as saying family members are missing but finally turns out that they are not missing, or we were taken on a bus but, finally, in the course of the treatment, it turned out that it was an unrealistic subjective perception. Did this often happen, or was the basic events for the trauma, was it usually kept, upheld during the treatment? And I'm just talking about the basic events, as I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Traumatic experiences are very difficult to express. It is very difficult to discuss one's pain and suffering, and people avoid it. In first contact with the traumatised people, their story is fragmented, interrupted, disjointed. One cannot reconstruct a story, a continuum, which could picture the real events --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Paint the real events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we succeed to have the person express verbally their pain and suffering, in order to create a continuous line of events, then we believe that, as of that moment on, that person is capable with coping with their current situation. However, one cannot use fragments to create an entire traumatic story. Once that story is set in place, then it -- it is no longer as traumatic. They are no longer afraid of discussing those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you have not fully understood my question. Because I'm not talking about create a continuous line but parts of a story which later turned out to be untrue. And I will give an example, which is totally foreign to this case, has got nothing to do with this case. But if someone would come to you a trauma, saying that it was caused by being raped, then I take it that it's possible that during the treatment, it finally turns out that there must be serious doubt or even the person himself says, "I was not raped." Now I'm seeking whether these basic events, such as being taken on a bus, or having lost three members of the family, whether, during the treatment it happened, or happened rarely, or never happened, or often happened, that, after some time, that person would say, "Well, my new reality is I was never taken on a bus," or, "The reality is that my family members are still alive and they're not missing." That's my question. I'm talking not about a continuous story but about very specific factual elements which we heard often about in this case, whether it's your experience that it turned out to be -- that the veracity of what they would have started telling you or what they have told you during the treatment later on turned out to be invented by that person but foreign to what really happened.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: In my experience, it did not take place. It does not. There was no need for them to do so. There was enough suffering and there was no need to add any more. It never happened that someone said that something happened and it turned out later that it had not. Many -- there were many things that they didn't mention at first because they could not even recall them. They had forgotten some. They were completely disassociated from such memories. But it never happened that anyone in such situation said something which turned out not to be true later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Ms. Hasan, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, I have no additional questions. But I would like to offer into evidence the excerpts from the witness's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do that, I have to ask Mr. Lukic whether the questions by the Bench have triggered any need for further questions. Not. Then you wanted to tender the -- Ms. Hasan could you be --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to tender 65 ter 29099, which is the prior testimony of Ms. Ibrahimefendic from the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object to this admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis -- is it ... What should that statement again be 94 or 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's tendered as a 92 ter statement. Because Ms. Hasan - at least that's how I understood it - was asking the confirmation or the attestation to that prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a 92 ter statement of an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the same objections we had before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will decide in due course on the objection and possibly the admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, pending -- depending on what the decision is, it may result in, you know, if it's not admitted, having to recall Ms. Ibrahimefendic to lead her on the matters addressed in her prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that that is a possibility. When I say "in due course," that could be very short and could be a bit longer. So, therefore, I would give us at least the next break to see whether we can already reach a decision or not. Whether or not reasons to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, you have followed the last discussion between the parties, that is, whether or not the Chamber should admit into evidence your previous testimony, to which often reference is made during your testimony of today. If we would not admit your testimony, that might cause the Prosecution to re-call you. We will try to deal with it as quickly as possible, but I can't give you any guarantees. It could be that within one hour from now the decision would there and therefore that the Prosecution would also know whether they would intend to re-call you. Under those circumstances, I have to ask you not to speak with anyone about your testimony given today, where there is a chance - I'm not expressing myself whether it's a 1 per cent or a 99 per cent chance - that you will be re-called. Is that instruction clear that you should not talk with anyone, not to communicate with anyone about your testimony up till the moment that you relieved from this limitation? It's clear to you, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber -- the Chamber is considering, as a matter of fact, to take a short break now and to see whether we can reach any decision in the next 20 minutes, which would then leave us another 65 minutes for the remainder of today's session. May I take it, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, that your travelling back does not start within the next hour or ... or do you intend to immediately move out from The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'll be staying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
