utterances.text: Yes. Then I think it would also be wise to ask Ms. Ibrahimefendic to be back in -- after the break so that she also knows what the consequences of the Chamber's decision most likely will be. We then, after Ms. Ibrahimefendic has left the courtroom ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd forgotten entirely about you, Ms. Marcus, and you said you needed only a few minutes. Perhaps it's very practical to use those four minutes now. Can we deal with the matter in open session or should we move into ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think this is a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Private session. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Ms. Ibrahimefendic be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, we have no further questions for you, but the Chamber wants to deliver its decision in relation to 65 ter 29099. The Chamber admits the previous testimony from the Krstic case into evidence, under Rule 92 ter. Reasons to follow. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29099 receives number P1800, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is therefore P1800, which is admitted into evidence. Ms. Ibrahimefendic, this also means that - I take it at least, Ms. Hasan, that there's no need to further consider any re-call of Ms. Ibrahimefendic - that this concludes your testimony. We'd like to thank you very much for having answered all the questions that were put to you, whether by the parties or by the Bench, and we wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher. And the usher may escort the next witness into the courtroom as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And Mr. McCloskey would also like to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as long as at least one counsel remains. Ms. Lee, you're in charge? And are you ready to call Mr. Lawrence?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lawrence, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite to you make it. The text is handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Lawrence, when you said "Dr. Lawrence," we have the habit of addressing everyone as Mr. or -- not in any way in depreciation of ranks or titles. We are fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee, if are you ready you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Ms. Lee. Ms. Lee is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find her to your right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Since you and I both speak the same language, I would ask that you pause between each question and answer so -- and wait for translation.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Christopher Hamilton Lawrence. That's L-a-w-r-e-n-c-e.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And, Dr. Lawrence, what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And do you recall testifying in the Krstic case before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And as well as the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And have you had the opportunity to review your testimony in those cases?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And the -- at that time when you were giving testimony, was it to the best of your knowledge and truthful?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today, would you provide the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender 92 ter transcripts and associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I have the 65 ter numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. It's 65 ter number 29100, and this is the excerpt from the -- from Dr. Lawrence's Krstic testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P1801, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: There is also 65 ter number 29101, and this is the excerpt from the Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P1802, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are also two associated exhibits that I would like that tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we first decide on admission of the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1801 and P1802 are admitted into evidence. Associated exhibits, Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 04574, which is the CV of Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, I take it. Then the next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Receives number P1804, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to read a summary of evidence of Dr. Lawrence, the purpose of which has been explained to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Christopher Lawrence is a certified forensic pathologist. From May through October 1998, he was the chief forensic pathologist for the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. Dr. Lawrence led a team who conducted autopsies on the human remains exhumed from several mass graves associated with the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, including the dam site near Petkovci, and seven secondary graves along Cancari road, Hodzici Road near Zeleni Jadar and Liplje. The autopsies were performed at a morgue in Visoko, Bosnia. The body bags delivered to Dr. Lawrence and his team at the morgue contained bodies in some cases and body parts in others. After photographing the contents of the body bags, the pathologists conducted a fluoroscopic examination of the remains for bullets, fractures, and boney abnormalities. They recovered personal items and removed clothing from the remains which were given to crime scene officers. Dr. Lawrence and his team then examined the bodies and bones and photographed any evidence of injury. Damaged bones were handed over to the anthropologists for reconstruction and then examined by pathologists for injury. In the case of an apparent gun-shot injury, attempts were made to trace the track of the bullet. In most instances, the pathologist also examined the clothing to determine whether the damage to the clothing was consistent with the injuries identified. Dr. Lawrence prepared a report for each grave-site containing his findings and his opinion as to the cause of death. In total, his team examined 2.239 body bags containing a minimum number of 883 individuals. The causes of death for the majority of the bodies found intact were gun-shot wounds. Some victims sustained gun-shot and shrapnel wounds. Most of the shrapnel wounds were sustained by victims recovered from the Zeleni Jadar secondary mass grave-site. During autopsy, Dr. Lawrence and his team retrieved 83 ligatures and 103 blindfolds. Most ligatures were tied around victims' wrists and arms. In many cases, blindfolds were found in position, covering the eyes of victims. And this concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any further questions for the witness you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, before I begin my questions, I see that you have brought some documents with you today. Could you describe to us what they are.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. They are copies of the reports that I prepared for the ICTY on the eight sites were examined and a summary document of the findings that I prepared for the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And if you wish to refer to these documents, please do so, but if you are referring to them, please let us know and let us know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, since your last testimony in the Karadzic in December of 2011, are you at the same job?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm still the state forensic pathologist for Tasmania.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And how long have you been there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Since 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And if you could describe to us very generally what your responsibilities are?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: My responsibilities as a state forensic pathologist are to carry out an autopsy service for the -- for the state coroner of Tasmania, to attend the scene of suspicious deaths, to advise the police on investigation of deaths, and to prepare reports on the deaths for the coroner, to prepare reports on suspicious cases for the courts, to -- and also to work on cases for the coroner in relation to deaths in hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Now, we mentioned a few minutes ago that you testified before this Tribunal in the Krstic and the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Have you -- did you testify as an expert in any other case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in Popovic and Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And have you testified as an expert anywhere --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would ask that the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And make a pause between question and answer and between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Have you testified as an expert witness in any other jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I have testified -- sorry. Yes, I have testified as an expert witness in Australia and in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And in what area of expertise or discipline did you testify as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: As a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And on how many occasions, approximately, did you testify as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Probably somewhere between 50 and 100 times.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Now, there is -- I'd like to ask you specific -- just a specific question relating to one particular case and this is R. versus Jeffrey Gilham.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: What was your involvement in that case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This -- sorry. This was a case that I examined in 1993. It was a triple homicide in which three people had been stabbed to death and the house had been burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Ms. Lee, the Chamber is wondering why these details are relevant. Of course, the Chamber has no knowledge about this case, et cetera. And ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: The -- I will be asking this witness about -- he had testified as an expert witness and we will get to that point very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, we are wondering why 50 to 100 testimonies are not sufficient information. Why we need go into the details of one case. But if you have any good reason, immediately go to that point, and -- I mean, the circumstances of that case seems not to be very relevant for us at this moment, unless, by your questioning, it becomes relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lawrence, in this case, did any issue arise as concerns to your evidence in that case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Sorry. Yes, it did. This was a complex case and had gone to -- to inquests to two trials and an appeal. Now the appeal was heard shortly before I gave evidence in the Karadzic trial. And the significance for the Court is that in the appeal it became clear to me that I had made an error in my assessment of the significance of some evidence in relation to a low level of carbon monoxide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you wanted to point that the expert witness is not a man without any failure in his life, then that has become clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Great. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Moving into a different area, I would like to now ask you about your involvement in Bosnia in 1998.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your chief -- you were the chief pathologist for the OTP at the ICTY; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And what is it that you were tasked to do?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I was tasked to run a mortuary to carry out autopsies on the bodies that were exhumed by the exhumation team in 1998, to ascertain the cause of death and, where possible, to collect evidence to identify the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And what were your main responsibilities? Did you have any supervisory role?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I supervised the team at the mortuary. I instructed the pathologists. I reviewed the reports, and I prepared summary reports on the cases that were found. In addition, I carried out quite a number of the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And you just testified that you reviewed the reports. Whose reports were they?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I reviewed a number of reports, the reports by the doctors and to some degree the reports of the anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And by "doctors," you mean other pathologists?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The other pathologists, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: So you just mentioned reports. Did you yourself write any reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I prepared the eight reports that I have with me today.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And these eight reports, they relate to each grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And they're namely the dam; the Cancari Road 3; Cancari Road 12; Hodzici Road 3, 4, 5; Zeleni Jadar 5; and Liplje 2?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Did you write any reports relating to these sites?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: As a consequence of our work at Cancari Road 3, we became aware that there may be a primary site at Kozluk. And at the end of September or perhaps early October, I attended a scene at Kozluk where we recovered a number of -- of two body bags of skeletal remains. And I prepared a report, a one-page report in response to that. I also prepared a report on some ligatures that had been recovered from the graves and had been sent to The Hague which had not examined in the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And did have you the opportunity review each of these reports that you prepared in relation to the Srebrenica events before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And do you still stand by the analysis and conclusions that you reached in those reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender these 11 reports, pursuant to Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please reserve 11 numbers and make a memo describing the 65 ter numbers, the short name of the report, and the numbers to be assigned. All 11 reports are admitted into evidence under the numbers Madam Registrar will assign in this memo.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And may I read out the 65 ter numbers for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please verify the list made by Madam Registrar, because I think they are on our list already so they don't have to be read out again. They're all in sequential order so if you would say the first and the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. It goes from 04576 until 04584, and then there are two additional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As appearing on this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: On the list, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And two additional ones are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They're the first two on the non-associated exhibits list. Madam Registrar will prepare the memo. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, in your reports, you determine a cause of death for each reported body bags as opposed to individual bodies, and can you briefly explain to us why they are assigned to body bags?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. The bodies that we were dealing with were largely recovered from secondary graves and in some of the graves, the bodies were not only significantly decomposed but also quite significantly disrupted. The consequence of this was that the -- it was not possible to examine entire bodies in -- in many cases. Some of the sites, for example, Hodzici 5, the bodies were quite well preserved, but in others, for example, the dam site or Liplje, the bodies were extremely disrupted. We therefore had to make an assessment about, did we provide only reports for entire bodies or did we provide reports for the entire bodies and the body bags. I made a decision to examine the body bags and the whole bodies, in order to record as much information as I could. This decision made some problems, because, obviously, incomplete bodies that cannot be linked to each other does raise the possibility that you might have multiple causes of death for one body. But I felt in the circumstances that it was important to document as many cases of gun-shot wounds as we could, given that the evidence that we were receiving from the clothing was that there were probably more gun-shot wounds than we were seeing. In the end, we mostly concentrated our efforts on the whole bodies because this was the most meaningful information, and the causes of death in the 254 intact bodies were probably the most useful pieces of information. But the problem was in many of the sites, and the dam site and Liplje particularly, there was so much damage that we were dealing with almost no intact bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to a different area, your reports mention blindfolds and ligatures.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 0 -- it's 65 ter number 04581. And this is -- at page 18. And this is Dr. Lawrence's report on the Hodzici Road 4 site. I believe we're having some technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The uploading of photographs takes some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially if they are in large series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar adds that the computer is slow anyhow today. Maybe due to the weather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're slowly getting to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, can you please describe to us what you see on this picture on your screen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. What you can see underneath the hand is the top part of a skull with a blindfold around the skull. Now, I should point out that this skull has been reconstructed and the blindfold has been positioned there after the skull has been reconstructed. But you can see where the arrow is, there is a gun-shot wound in the left temple region and there is a corresponding defect in the blindfold, indicating that the blindfold was at that position when the gun-shot wound [sic] was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And when you say the skull has been reconstructed, who reconstructed the skull?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The skull was reconstructed by the anthropologists from the fragments of bone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the reconstruction and the glue, everything is in the -- already admitted testimony, Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, you previously testified about the difference between probable, possible, and definite gun-shot wounds. And I'm referring to -- I'm referring to P1802 at pages 6 to 9 in e-court. Now, how would you define the injuries shown here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Well, the injuries shown in this one, I would say this is a definite gun-shot wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 04582 at page 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And while this picture is loading, I would like to ask you, you also talk about ligatures that were found in the grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And what types of ligatures --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: There were --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: -- did you find?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: There were a number of different types of ligatures found. There tended to be particular types of ligatures found in particular graves but the ligatures included ligatures made from twine, ligatures that were made from a white fabric with an embroidered flower on them, white cloth, and a fabric which had coloured lines on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And if I could actually have page 16 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Doctor, can you describe us what you see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. What you can see on the screen is a fairly intact body, which is lying on its back. At the bottom, you can see the belt, which is slightly pulled down. Above that, you can see the hands, and the hands are secured with a cord ligature. And on the wrist, you can see a watch, a Seiko self-winding watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your description now is not the same as appears in the text below the -- could you please read that and see which of the two ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said the body is lying on its back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. The body is lying on its front. You can see the back. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And what would you say the -- would you be able to determine the cause of death in this situation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This one, there were gun-shot wounds in the right pelvis and bullet fragments in the right and left knees -- right and left thighs and knees. I'd need to refer -- for this specific case, I would need to refer to my list to ascertain it, but I would assume it would probably be given as cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 4578, at page 30 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And in terms of ligatures found, you had listed a number of ligatures --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: It's page 30. It's the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, you've mentioned different ligatures, and you had mentioned that you had written two reports on it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this ligature?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. These are the white ligatures with the embroidered flower and leaf on them. And these were seen in CR12 and CR13.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Is it CR13?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry, CR12 and CR3, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, for your reference, this particular ligature is also referenced in P1771 at e-court page 29, which was a report that was tendered through the textile expert Suzanna Maljaars, who previously testified earlier this week. And may I please have page 35 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And while the document is being uploaded, Dr. Lawrence, did you observe any bodies that had both blindfolds and ligatures?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. There were two bodies in CR12 that had both blindfolds and ligatures. They were body bag -- they were bodies 116 and body 121.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And can you -- looking at the picture in front of you, can you please describe to us what you see here.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This photograph shows the -- the skin from the right temple and there is in fact a bullet-hole between the fingers there which was also present in the blindfold.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Now, you've previously testified about -- actually, in this case like this, what would you determine this cause -- is this a case where you would be able to determine the cause of injury?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. A gun-shot wound in the head is going to kill you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And is this a definite gun-shot wound?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And, Dr. Lawrence, you have also testified about possible or probable cause of death and definite cause of death, and this is in relation to P1802 at pages 9 and 10. In this case, is this a case where a definite cause of death could be established?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Lee. Mr. Lawrence, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, before we begin with my questions, I would like to again remind you and caution you that since we both speak the same language, we have to try and observe a pause between my question and your answer to allow the other persons in this courtroom to do their job. Is that fair, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I will try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that in addition to your medical training and degree you also studied law after becoming a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I studied law while I was becoming a pathologist, but I did not complete my training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to your testimony that you have provided for us here and in the reports that you authored for purposes of reporting the work you did in Bosnia, did you wear an attorney hat at all or was this exclusively your medical forensic pathologist hat that you were reporting under?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I do not profess to a be lawyer. I am forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And am I also correct that at some point in time you did take, I think, two courses, one in the US, in forensic anthropology; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take it that this participation in two courses did not result in any earned degree in forensic anthropology; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. I would regard myself as a forensic pathologist with an interest in forensic anthropology, not a forensic anthropologist [Realtime transcript read in error "pathologist"].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And now, Doctor, I don't want you to take this the wrong way insofar as it's not intended to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt for a moment. There's a wrong entry in the transcript at line 11. "Not a forensic anthropologist," you said, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, again, Doctor, I don't want you to take this the wrong way. It is not meant as a criticism of you, but in fact, being the state forensic pathologist for Tasmania, are you also the only forensic pathologist in Tasmania?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. There is it a second forensic pathologist who also trained at the office of the medical investigator in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would that be the individual that you recruited about -- a couple years ago?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that generally speaking in the field of work of forensic review of mortal remains, anthropologists usually have more of a role as to remains that are fully skeletonised, whereas a forensic pathologist would have more of a role where the remains have soft tissue present?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: As a general rule, that's correct. The amount of forensic anthropology available varies from area to area. Forensic anthropology is probably better developed in the United States than it is, say, in England. I think it would be fair to say now if we were carrying out this examination, then most of the work would be done by the forensic anthropologists. In this -- in -- at this period, it was done by both in consultation, and there are certain values in that in as far as because these bodies were quite badly decomposed, it was sometimes necessary to work out where the bullets would have travelled and that sometimes better done by forensic pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the work that was done in this case or I should say in these cases since there were a number of reports about different sites, am I correct that the pathologists, and that would be you, had the final decision or say regarding the assessment of the injuries?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And ... and in regard to the type of consultations that you would have had with the anthropologists in terms of coming to a conclusion, I would like to take a look at something with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's 1D1142 and it will be page 34 in e-court, which will correlate to transcript page 7403 of the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And once that comes up on the monitors, sir, I would invite you to follow along as I read lines 6 through 22 and then I'll have some questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please the 1D number again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, it's a little bit faint on my screen but I think that's the page, and if we can follow along from line 6, the question was: "Since you said that the pathologist's findings were final and authoritative, can you tell what could then have been the cause of such disagreement? Do you have an example? And was there one single uniform model for making reports? Or was it possible that injuries were described differently from report to report? "A. That's a multi-part question. The pathologists varied in their experience of dealing with boney injuries. And most of the pathologists would listen to the anthropologists' opinions in these cases."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. "I can recall some discussions between myself and Mr. Baraybar in relation to some of the injuries that would be classified as possible or probable gun-shot wounds. For example, where you might have a defect that didn't have all of the normal characteristics of a gun-shot wound but might have some fragments of metal. Those are the sorts of things that might occur. There were also occasional questions about whether there was a blunt force injury, a fracturing, which was -- and whether it was, in fact, a blunt force or whatever [sic] it was -- occurred as a consequence of a gun-shot wound."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, first I'm going to ask you does this appear to accurately depict the testimony as you recall --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out the "blunt force or whatever it was," I think that's page 25, it should read "whether it was" and not "whatever it was."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say the pathologists varied in their experience as to boney injuries, I assume there we're talking about the other medical pathologists that would have been working on the team and would have been performing some of the autopsies as to the remains that were recovered?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that certain parts of your report such as the determination of a minimum number of individuals and other anthropological data within them, for those parts you're in essence entirely relying upon the information that was conveyed to by the anthropologists? You're not making any personal opinions in those aspects of your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- sorry. Yes, the only reason the information appears at all is because it's -- it's necessary to make sense of some of the observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct, sir, that you did not have a personal role in the exhumation and removal of the bodies, that this was performed by Dr. Richard Wright and his team?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Wright was in charge of the exhumation team. I did attend the exhumations at CR12, CR3, Liplje, and Zeleni Jadar, but only to have a -- only to look at what was there. Richard was responsible for what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the actual autopsy work that was performed in these cases am I -- would I be correct in stating that you personally carried out only about one fifth to one quarter of all the autopsies that were performed during your tenure as chief pathologist to the ICTY mission?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And am I also correct that at most times there were three and then later maybe four pathologists working simultaneously at any given time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned something about reviewing the work of the other pathologists. Was it the case that you would review every single autopsy report that was prepared by another pathologist or would there be a selection process? How did that review by yourself -- how did that take place?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Initially I reviewed every single report. Towards the end as we grew larger, I reviewed all of the whole body reports and all of the large and significant body part reports. That's how I compiled the information for the summary reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of your review of the report, would that entail also an independent review of the remains that are the subject of the report by yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And ... in each of the reports authored by you, the summary reports, we always find something to the effect of saying that each autopsy is entirely the responsibility of the pathologist performing the autopsy and that at the end of the paragraph there's usually verbiage stating that the opinions expressed in the report are entirely those of the pathologist concerned. In that sense, sir, the summary report, is it summarising the findings of those pathologists who prepared the autopsies, including in those cases where you prepared the autopsy, those findings, or is it reporting on what your review of the reports found?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: It was -- it was pretty much what the pathologists said. There may have been occasional cases where having reviewed the documentation, the thermal images of the x-rays, I might disagree. The report remained -- the original report remained the same. My summary report would reflect what I thought of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with the general proposition that neither a prosecutor nor investigator should ever have a role in instructing a forensic pathologist how to draft their autopsy report or what to list as a cause of death?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the reports that you prepared, am I correct that you have not done any further work on these matters since the time of the trial in the Krstic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you permit, sir, that developments that have occurred since your work on the case may cast a new light on the facts that were known to you at the time and thus might change the conclusions that were reached?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the break. I'm about to go on to another topic, so we could take a break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll even adjourn for the day. Mr. Lawrence, before we do so, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony given today or testimony still to be given. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 19th of July, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.
